title: Longest Nice Substring
statement:
Call a string *nice* when each letter in it shows up in both forms: whenever the lowercase letter occurs, so does its uppercase partner, and the other way round. For instance `"cCdDc"` is nice, while `"cCd"` is not, since `'d'` occurs without `'D'`.

Given `s`, return the longest substring (contiguous part) of `s` that is nice. If several nice substrings share the greatest length, return the one that starts earliest in `s`. If no substring is nice, return the empty string `""`.
constraints: s contains only uppercase and lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

Checking every substring works for 100 characters, but there is a neater idea. If some character of `s` has no partner of the other case anywhere in `s`, no nice substring can contain it, because the partner is missing from every substring too. So that character splits `s` into a left piece and a right piece, and the answer lies entirely inside one of them. Solve both pieces the same way (divide and conquer). If every character has its partner, `s` itself is nice.

## Approach

1. A string shorter than 2 cannot be nice, so return `""`.
2. Put the characters of `s` in the set `present`.
3. Scan `s` for the first character `ch` whose lowercase or uppercase form is missing from `present`.
4. If one is found at index `i`, solve `before` = the part left of `i` and `after` = the part right of `i`, and return the longer one, preferring `before` on a tie because it starts earlier.
5. If no character is missing a partner, return `s`.

## Example 1, step by step

`s = "YazaAay"` has `present = {Y, a, z, A, y}`. `'Y'` and `'a'` have partners, but `'z'` (index 2) has no `'Z'`. The left piece `"Ya"` splits at `'Y'` (no `'y'` there) into two pieces too short to be nice, so `before = ""`. The right piece `"aAay"` splits at `'y'` into `"aAa"`, where every character has its partner, so `after = "aAa"`. It is longer than `before`, so the answer is `"aAa"`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n²) in the worst case: every call scans its piece in O(n), and each call either finishes or removes one character, so there are O(n) calls.
- Space: O(n²) in the worst case for the nested slices on the recursion stack; tiny for n ≤ 100.

## Pitfalls

- The partner check must use the whole current piece, not the original `s`: in `"Ya"`, `'Y'` has no partner even though `'y'` exists elsewhere.
- On equal lengths keep `before`; choosing `after` breaks the earliest-start rule (`"dDzeE"` must give `"dD"`).
- A single character is never nice, so `"c"` gives `""`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `present` | set of characters in the current piece |
| `i`, `ch` | index and character being checked |
| `before` | best nice substring left of the splitting character |
| `after` | best nice substring right of it |

narration.2: Fewer than two characters can never be nice.
narration.3: Such a piece has no nice substring at all.
narration.5: Collect the characters of this piece for quick lookups.
narration.6: Scan the piece for a character without its partner.
narration.8: Both its lowercase and uppercase forms occur in this piece?
narration.9: Then it may belong to a nice substring; keep scanning.
narration.11: It has no partner, so no nice substring crosses it: solve the part on its left...
narration.13: Keep the longer answer; on a tie the left one starts earlier.
narration.15: Every character has its partner, so the whole piece is nice.
